title: Thermal Pleasure and Alliesthesia in the Built Environment

findings.mechanism: Alliesthesia operates within the thermoneutral zone, without requiring core temperature deviation.
findings.quote: positive alliesthesia occurs within the physiological thermoneutral zone

findings.antecedent: corrective temperature step-change (physiological load error incurred)
findings.mechanism: Pleasure increases proportionally to the physiological load error incurred.
findings.quote: The intensity of thermal pleasure immediately following a corrective temperature step-change increased proportionally to the physiological load error incurred

findings.mechanism: No significant change in thermal pleasure was registered.
findings.quote: No change in thermal pleasure (Tples) was registered by subjects during Sequence A1

findings.mechanism: A small decrease in thermal pleasure was observed.
findings.quote: only a small decrease in Sequence B1.

findings.antecedent: mild displeasure (negative Tples) preceding local stimulation (fan in A2 or heat lamps in B2)
findings.mechanism: Local stimulation generated a positive change in hedonic tone after mild displeasure.
findings.quote: Mild displeasure (negative Tples) preceded the initiation of behavioural control actions for Sequence A2 and B2, but local stimulation generated a positive change in hedonic tone.

findings.antecedent: radiant heating from heat lamps in cool environment (Sequence B2)
findings.mechanism: Radiant heating was effective in minimizing body heat loss and sustaining thermal pleasure.
findings.quote: thermal pleasure was sustained for the duration of the exposure.

findings.antecedent: Sequences A4 (exercise + cool down) and B4 (cold exposure + warm up)
findings.consequent: positive increments in thermal pleasure votes
findings.mechanism: These sequences elicited the largest positive increments in thermal pleasure.
findings.quote: Clearly the largest positive increments in thermal pleasure votes were registered after Sequences A4 and B4.

findings.mechanism: A strong negative correlation was found for warm exposures (Sequences A1–A4).
findings.quote: A Pearson correlation indicated a strong negative correlation between the change in skin temperature and the change in thermal pleasure (r = −0.66; p < 0.01) for the warm exposures (Sequences A1–A4)

findings.mechanism: A strong positive correlation was found for cool exposures (Sequences B1–B4).
findings.quote: and a strong positive correlation (r = 0.65; p < 0.01) for the cool exposures (Sequences B1–B4).

findings.antecedent: localized convective cooling (fan) applied to the back of the subject in Sequence A2
findings.mechanism: Increased thermal pleasure for approximately seven minutes.
findings.quote: Localized convective cooling applied to the back of the subject in Sequence A2 increased thermal pleasure for approximately seven minutes

findings.antecedent: local skin temperature changing in opposing direction to mean skin temperature
findings.mechanism: This phenomenon is termed 'spatial alliesthesia'.
findings.quote: There was a positive change in thermal pleasure ratings as local skin temperature changed in the opposing direction to the mean condition.

findings.antecedent: mean and local skin temperatures converging (Sequence A1)
findings.mechanism: Displeasure occurred due to diminishing efficacy of convective cooling.
findings.quote: Displeasure occurred in Sequence A1 as mean and local skin temperatures converged because of the diminishing efficacy of convective cooling

findings.antecedent: heat lamps in cool environment (Sequence B2) maintaining divergent skin temperatures
findings.mechanism: Divergent skin temperatures sustained positive alliesthesia for ten minutes.
findings.quote: the heat lamps in Sequence B2 maintained divergent skin temperatures and positive alliesthesia was sustained for ten minutes.

findings.antecedent: corrective transitions within the thermoneutral zone (Sequences 1-3)
findings.mechanism: Core temperature changes were negligible or non-existent, dismissing the notion that thermal discomfort is a necessary precondition for positive thermal alliesthesia.
findings.quote: The subjects of this experiment reported positive pleasure following corrective transitions within the thermoneutral zone (Figure 7) where core temperature changes were negligible or non-existent (Figure 5).

findings.mechanism: Local warming had a significant increase on global thermal sensation.
findings.quote: Applying local warming had a significant increase (p < 0.05) on global (whole-body) thermal sensation (Tsens,g) for both feet and hand warming.

findings.mechanism: Local warming had a significant increase on global thermal sensation.
findings.quote: Applying local warming had a significant increase (p < 0.05) on global (whole-body) thermal sensation (Tsens,g) for both feet and hand warming.

findings.consequent: distinction between global (Tsens,g) and local (Tsens,l) sensation
findings.mechanism: Subjects could distinguish between global and local sensation.
findings.quote: subjects could distinguish between their global sensation (Tsens,g) and their local sensation (Tsens,l) during periods of thermal stimulation of the feet and hands.

findings.consequent: distinction between global (Tsens,g) and local (Tsens,l) sensation
findings.mechanism: Subjects could distinguish between global and local sensation.
findings.quote: subjects could distinguish between their global sensation (Tsens,g) and their local sensation (Tsens,l) during periods of thermal stimulation of the feet and hands.

findings.consequent: mean pre- and post-onset thermal pleasure (Tples)
findings.mechanism: The mean pre- and post-onset thermal pleasure was not significantly different, indicating variability in individual responses.
findings.quote: pre- and post-onset Tples was not significantly different

findings.mechanism: Minimum thermal pleasure was significantly lower than pre-onset.
findings.quote: Pre-onset,Tples 0.71 ± 0.90 Post-onset,Tples,min −0.25 ± 0.84∗ t(27) = 5.30

findings.mechanism: Maximum thermal pleasure was significantly higher than pre-onset.
findings.quote: Pre-onset,Tples 0.71 ± 0.90 Post-onset,Tples,max 1.73 ± 0.83∗ t(27) = −6.88

findings.mechanism: Minimum thermal pleasure was significantly lower than pre-onset.
findings.quote: Pre-onset,Tples 0.49 ± 0.99 Post-onset,Tples,min −0.56 ± 0.78∗ t(45) = 7.70

findings.mechanism: Maximum thermal pleasure was significantly higher than pre-onset.
findings.quote: Pre-onset,Tples 0.49 ± 0.99 Post-onset,Tples,max 1.02 ± 0.94∗ t(45) = −4.01

findings.mechanism: Local stimulation produced a highly significant non-zero change in hedon units, indicating a significant effect on pleasure.
findings.quote: local stimulation produced a highly significant (p < 0.01) non-zero change in hedon units for both foot warming (t(27) = 4.973) and hand warming (t(46) = 7.899).

findings.consequent: predominantly positive change in thermal pleasure votes
findings.mechanism: 59% of participants experienced positive pleasure.
findings.quote: When heating was applied locally to the foot, 59% of participants experienced a predominantly positive change in thermal pleasure votes

findings.consequent: predominantly positive change in thermal pleasure votes
findings.mechanism: 37% of participants experienced positive pleasure.
findings.quote: Hand warming only had a predominantly positive effect on 37% of participants.

findings.mechanism: MANOVA showed a statistically significant difference in hedonic response.
findings.quote: There was a statistically significant difference in hedonic response based on the identified alliesthesial variables for both the onset (F(4,53) = 11.779, p = 0.000; Wilks’s x = 0.53)

findings.mechanism: MANOVA showed a statistically significant difference in hedonic response.
findings.quote: and the tail periods (F(4,53) = 3.80, p = 0.009; Wilks’s x = 0.78).

findings.consequent: positive hedonic trend during onset period
findings.mechanism: Participants with a positive hedonic trend had lower pre-onset Tples.
findings.quote: pre-onset Tples... significantly different between clusters during the onset period of warming. Participants with a positive hedonic trend during the onset period had lower local skin temperatures

findings.consequent: positive hedonic trend during onset period
findings.mechanism: Participants with a positive hedonic trend had cooler pre-onset local skin temperatures.
findings.quote: pre-onset Tsk,l... significantly different between clusters during the onset period of warming. Participants with a positive hedonic trend during the onset period had lower local skin temperatures

findings.consequent: positive hedonic trend during onset period
findings.mechanism: Participants with a positive hedonic trend experienced more local warming.
findings.quote: ΔTsk,l after 3 min were significantly different between clusters during the onset period of warming. Participants with a positive hedonic trend during the onset period... received more local warming in the first 3 min

findings.consequent: negative hedonic trend during tail period
findings.mechanism: Subjects with a negatively trending ΔTples had warmer pre-onset skin temperature.
findings.quote: Subjects with a negatively trending ΔTples during the tail period had a warmer pre-onset skin temperature

findings.consequent: negative hedonic trend during tail period
findings.mechanism: Subjects with a negatively trending ΔTples experienced a larger magnitude of local warming.
findings.quote: and experienced a larger magnitude of local warming after 5 min than those with a positive trend.

findings.mechanism: The model was highly significant and explained 60% of the variance in hedonic response.
findings.quote: Both models for the onset (x2(3) = 34.75, p = 0.000)... were highly significant. The onset model explained 60% (Nagelkerke R2) of the variance in hedonic response

findings.mechanism: The model was highly significant but less successful at explaining variance.
findings.quote: and tail period (x2(2) = 10.74, p = 0.005) were highly significant... whilst the tail model was less successful at 23% (Nagelkerke R2).

findings.consequent: likelihood of negative hedonic response (onset period)
findings.mechanism: Higher pre-onset pleasure increases the likelihood of a negative hedonic response to local warming.
findings.quote: the likelihood of a participant in this experiment having a negative hedonic response from local warming in the onset period was 3.18 times greater per unit increase in pre-onset Tples.

findings.consequent: likelihood of negative hedonic response (onset period)
findings.mechanism: Warmer pre-onset local skin temperature increases the likelihood of a negative hedonic response.
findings.quote: the change in odds from the observed difference in pre-onset Tsk,l accounted for the largest increase in the odds of a negative hedonic response from local warming during the onset period.

findings.consequent: likelihood of negative hedonic response (onset period)
findings.mechanism: An increase in ΔTsk,l reduces the likelihood of a negative response.
findings.quote: A 1°C increase in ΔTsk,l after 3 min reduced the likelihood of a negative response during the onset period.

findings.consequent: likelihood of negative hedonic response (tail period)
findings.mechanism: Warmer pre-onset local skin temperature increases the likelihood of a negative hedonic response.
findings.quote: Pre-stimulusTsk,l 1.37

findings.consequent: likelihood of negative hedonic response (tail period)
findings.mechanism: Higher levels of local heating after 5 min increase the likelihood of a negative response.
findings.quote: the participants receiving higher levels of local heating after 5 min being twice as likely to respond negatively.

findings.antecedent: intensity of subjects’ displeasure in the preconditioning environment
findings.consequent: tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure response to localised thermal stimuli
findings.mechanism: This was the most useful variable for distinguishing the pleasure response.
findings.quote: The most useful variable for distinguishing the tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure response to localised thermal stimuli was the intensity of the subjects’ displeasure in the preconditioning environment.

findings.antecedent: magnitude of change in local skin temperature
findings.consequent: perceived pleasantness of localised thermal stimuli
findings.mechanism: A significant effect was observed.
findings.quote: The magnitude of change in local skin temperature also had a significant effect on perceived pleasantness of localised thermal stimuli.

findings.mechanism: Elevated air movement significantly increased thermal pleasure.
findings.quote: elevated air movement significantly increased average thermal pleasure (F(2.973,80.267) = 22.349, p < 0.0005)

findings.mechanism: Elevated air movement significantly decreased skin temperature.
findings.quote: significantly decreased skin temperature (F(3.057,103.936) = 121.737, p < 0.0005)

findings.mechanism: Elevated air movement significantly decreased thermal sensation compared to pre-fan votes.
findings.quote: thermal sensation significantly decreased (F(4,136) = 14.768, p < 0.0005) when compared with pre-fan votes

findings.antecedent: different air movement patterns (constant, sinusoidal, square-wave, saw-tooth)
findings.mechanism: No significant differences were found between the air movement patterns.
findings.quote: post-hoc comparisons using Bonferroni correction found there were no significant perceptual or physiological differences (p < 0.05) between the air movement patterns.

findings.consequent: peak rate of change in skin temperature (dTsk)
findings.mechanism: The peak rate of change in skin temperature was significantly greater in the first sequence.
findings.quote: the peak rate of change in skin temperature (dTsk) was also significantly greater in the first sequence (p < 0.005).

findings.consequent: change in thermal sensation from elevated air movement
findings.mechanism: Highly correlated, indicating that initial sensation influences the change.
findings.quote: subjects’ pre-fan psychometric votes of thermal sensation (r = −0.894, n = 28, p = 0.000) and thermal pleasure (r = −0.552, n = 28, p = 0.002) were highly correlated with the change in respective votes resulting from elevated air movement

findings.consequent: change in thermal pleasure from elevated air movement
findings.mechanism: Highly correlated, indicating that initial pleasure influences the change.
findings.quote: subjects’ pre-fan psychometric votes of thermal sensation (r = −0.894, n = 28, p = 0.000) and thermal pleasure (r = −0.552, n = 28, p = 0.002) were highly correlated with the change in respective votes resulting from elevated air movement

findings.consequent: change in thermal sensation after fans
findings.mechanism: Subjects who reported feeling warm had a larger change in thermal sensation.
findings.quote: Subjects who reported feeling warm during the period without fans had a larger change in thermal sensation vote after fans were switched on.

findings.consequent: positive shift in thermal pleasure from elevated air movement
findings.mechanism: Subjects experiencing mild displeasure had a greater positive shift in thermal pleasure.
findings.quote: Subjects experiencing mild displeasure in the pre-fan conditions had a greater positive shift in thermal pleasure under elevated air movement than those who were indifferent to the warm, still conditions.

findings.antecedent: psychophysiological variables (pre-fan thermal pleasure, change in neck skin temperature, change in thermal sensation, pre-fan neck skin temperature)
findings.consequent: magnitude of pleasure response to elevated air movement (clusters)
findings.mechanism: MANOVA showed significant differences between clusters based on these variables.
findings.quote: A multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was run to test for any significant differences in key physiological or psychometric variables between clusters. Four variables relevant to the spatial alliesthesia hypothesis were tested: pre-fan thermal pleasure, change in neck skin temperature from fans, change in thermal sensation from fans, and pre-fan neck skin temperature. The result of the MANOVA reported in Figure 10 indicates that there were two variables that were significantly different (F(4,23) = 5.417, p = 0.003; Wilk’s Λ = 0.52) between the two groups of the subjects.

findings.consequent: magnitude of pleasure response to elevated air movement (clusters)
findings.mechanism: Pre-fan thermal pleasure votes were the most significant difference between clusters.
findings.quote: The most significant difference between clusters was the pre-fan thermal pleasure votes (p < 0.01).

findings.antecedent: convective heat loss on the neck (greater)
findings.mechanism: Subjects with a modest change in thermal pleasure experienced significantly greater convective heat loss.
findings.quote: convective heat loss on the neck was significantly greater (p < 0.05) for the subjects with a modest change in thermal pleasure.

findings.antecedent: intensity of subjects’ displeasure in the preconditioning environment
findings.consequent: tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure reported by subjects
findings.mechanism: This was the most important variable distinguishing the pleasure response.
findings.quote: the most important variable distinguishing the tone and magnitude of thermal pleasure reported by subjects was the intensity of their displeasure in the preconditioning environment.

stimuli.description: Temperature step-changes and ramps (e.g., 24.5°C to 28°C, 24.5°C to 20°C), localized air movement (fan, 0.5 m/s), infrared radiant heat (heat lamps, 275W each), localized warming to hands and feet via Peltier cells, four air movement patterns (constant, sinusoidal, square-wave, saw-tooth) at 0.4-0.9 m/s targeted at the back of the neck.
stimuli.source: Paper 2, Figure 1 & 2; Paper 3, Figure 2 & 3; Paper 4, Figure 2 & 3
